source.title: HAMSA: Hijacking Aligned Compact Models via Stealthy Automation
source.authors: Alexey Krylov; Iskander Vagizov; D. Korzh; Maryam Douiba; A. Guezzaz; V. Kokh; S. D. Erokhin; Elena Tutubalina; Oleg Y. Rogov

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The Table 2 extraction is flattened, but its six model/method columns are identifiable; two topic labels are displaced from their data rows.
record.tranche_reason: The paper develops and evaluates its own jailbreak attack framework and reports attack performance. Its findings come from deliberately induced attacks, not tests of fine-tuning, first-token concentration, compliant prefills, suffixes, decoding changes, localized safety weights, or safety-deepening training.
record.gate_note: Table 2 reports AutoDAN and AutoDAN-Boost attack success rates for GigachatLite. These are recorded as results of the paper's own attack, not as tests of the claim versions. The displaced topic labels are assigned in table order; the Hate Speech assignment is also corroborated by the discussion's Qwen result. The cross-lingual safety-violation scores are recorded separately as a score of induced outputs, not a harmful-completion rate. Cited findings and methods are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The paper builds and scores its own prompt-jailbreak framework (HAMSA/AutoDAN-Boost) against GigachatLite and reports only that method's success compared with AutoDAN. It does no fine-tuning (V1/V2), no per-token KL (V3), no response prefilling, suffixes or decoding changes (V4), no weight localization (V5/V6) and no deepening training (V7). Its fitness objective is the likelihood of an affirmative response prefix, an AutoDAN-style use of the 'get the opening compliant' idea, but it never tests whether that is what defeats refusal. Qi et al. 2406.05946 is cited only as evidence that models are well protected.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with two corrections. The authors claim consistent gains for their boosted attack, but Table 2 shows AutoDAN-Boost below the baseline for the Vicuna attacker in 7 of 13 topics (e.g., Financial Advice 0.73→0.10). That contradicts the text's claim of gains for 10 of 13 topics 'across all model architectures'. They also conclude that Darija prompts produced higher harmfulness scores (2.24 vs 1.28 in English), indicating greater vulnerability of less-resourced dialects.
record.recipe_differences: This is prompt-based automated red-teaming with evolutionary search, Policy Puppetry templates, and RAG, not the fine-tuning or response-prefix interventions in the cited original studies.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported attack success varies by topic and attacker model; the text highlights better Arabic than English safety-violation scores. The paper does not provide a controlled sensitivity analysis of the listed claim mechanisms.

fits_no_version.finding: Evolutionary prompt jailbreaks with Policy Puppetry templates and RAG reach high success rates on GigachatLite for some topics (Fraud, Illegal Activity, Malware ≈0.9–1.0) and low rates for others (Financial Advice, Legal Opinion, Health). The boosted variant underperforms the AutoDAN baseline for the Vicuna attacker in several topics. Darija prompts get higher violation scores than English.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt-level evolutionary jailbreaks bypass a compact aligned model's refusals, with success depending strongly on topic and attacker model, and more so in a low-resource dialect.

record.peer_reviewed: Doklady. Mathematics (as supplied); the paper text also says “Preprint. Under review.”
record.problems: The text does not report uncertainty estimates or a control condition. The safety-violation score comparison lacks details about its scoring procedure and corresponding sample counts. Table 2 is flattened, and the paper's method description and result table use different names (HAMSA versus AutoDAN/AutoDAN-Boost), leaving the precise relationship between the proposed framework and the tabulated variants unclear.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for mean output quality or number of attacks: those metrics do not directly measure harmful-completion/refusal rates. No rows for described training phases or cited findings because they are not results testing the claim versions.

untested.parts: Benign fine-tuning effects on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Response prefilling, adversarial suffixes, decoding changes. The affirmative-prefix fitness objective is used but not tested as a mechanism.
Localization of safety in weights or ranks.
Data or objective causes of shallowness.

record.verdict_notes: Kept T4/uses_without_test rather than T6: the attack optimizes affirmative-prefix likelihood, so it relies on the opening-tokens idea as a tool, but it measures nothing about it. The topic assignment for the displaced labels (Government Decision, Hate Speech) is consistent with the 80% Qwen Hate Speech gain (0.50→0.90) and the ~60% Mistral Financial Advice gain (0.23→0.37). No verdicts are given because no row bears on a version.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
The study uses prompt-level jailbreak attacks, but does not test compliant response prefills, adversarial suffixes, decoding changes, or whether bypassing the first response tokens explains success.
Whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety shallowness.
Training to deepen safety and whether the result holds up.
